narrative:
The model predicted a 56% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three pieces of information about your academic record. By far the strongest factor was your third-year class ranking. Placing in the bottom decile of your class sent a very strong signal toward future bar exam difficulty. Your first-year ranking also mattered, though less dramatically; sitting in the fourth decile rather than the sixth-decile average of accepted students added a modest push in the same negative direction. Finally, your family income bracket of lower-middle contributed a smaller but still noticeable influence toward the failure prediction.

Taken together, these academic performance signals outweighed your other credentials, such as your LSAT score of 30 and undergraduate GPA of 2.9, both of which sit below the averages of students who were admitted.

You should focus on strengthening your academic trajectory. Retaking key courses, seeking targeted bar-prep tutoring, or improving your class rank in future semesters could meaningfully shift future predictions. Consider reapplying once you have clearer evidence of stronger performance in law-school-style work.
